items.headline: OpenAI’s new reasoning technique alarms AI safety experts
items.dek: OpenAI's new Astra model will use "recurrent depth," a technique that allows it to operate outside sequential thinking, making the model's chain of thought harder to monitor.
items.author: Russell Brandom
items.caption: TechCrunch hero: headline over green panel with OpenAI logo photo, byline Russell Brandom, Sept 2 2026
items.notes: Quotes in article: Buck Shlegeris (Redwood CEO): "...if OpenAI pushes this technique further, they'll have the option to massively increase the recurrence and totally destroys CoT monitorability." Ryan Greenblatt: "My biggest concern is that a natural progression from here would involve scaling up the opaque reasoning to the point where the model reasons entirely or almost entirely in latent space." Jakub Pachocki: "OpenAI has worked to preserve and utilize chain-of-thought monitoring since our very first reasoning models."

items.headline: GPT-6 Astra might be too powerful to understand or control
items.dek: OpenAI is hailing its new model as “the world’s most intelligent and aligned”, but the details reveal an awareness of being evaluated and an ability to manipulate its visible reasoning
items.author: Celia Ford
items.caption: Transformer (Substack) post header: headline, subtitle, byline Celia Ford, Sep 04 2026
items.notes: Quotes system card: "Astra shows a substantial decrease in chain-of-thought monitorability compared to previous models." and "If the model were to try to sandbag covertly, we would likely be unable to catch it." Tomek Korbak (OpenAI): "I am deeply worried by the trend of decreasing CoT monitorability."

items.headline: Chain of Thought Monitorability: A New and Fragile Opportunity for AI Safety
items.dek: AI systems that "think" in human language offer a unique opportunity for AI safety: we can monitor their chains of thought (CoT) for the intent to misbehave. ... Because CoT monitorability may be fragile, we recommend that frontier model developers consider the impact of development decisions on CoT monitorability.
items.author: Korbak, Balesni, Barnes, Bengio, ... Pachocki, ... Shah, Mikulik (41 authors from OpenAI, Google DeepMind, Anthropic, Meta, UK AISI, Redwood, Apollo, METR etc.)
items.caption: arXiv abstract page showing title, the long cross-lab author list (Bengio, Hendrycks, Kokotajlo, Legg, Pachocki, Zaremba, Mark Chen, ...) and abstract
items.notes: Joint OpenAI/DeepMind/Anthropic position paper. Endorsed by Hinton, Sutskever, Sam Bowman, John Schulman (per VentureBeat).

items.headline: OpenAI, Google DeepMind and Anthropic sound alarm: 'We may be losing the ability to understand AI'
items.dek: Scientists from OpenAI, Google DeepMind, Anthropic and Meta have abandoned their fierce corporate rivalry to issue a joint warning about AI safety. More than 40 researchers across these competing companies published a research paper today arguing that a brief window to monitor AI reasoning could close forever — and soon.
items.author: Michael Nuñez
items.caption: Headline text only (page rendered without CSS in headless browser)
items.notes: Quote (Bowen Baker, OpenAI): "The existing CoT monitorability may be extremely fragile. Higher-compute RL, alternative model architectures, certain forms of process supervision, may all lead to models that obfuscate their thinking."

items.headline: AI Is Scheming, and Stopping It Won’t Be Easy, OpenAI Study Finds
items.author: Tharin Pillay and Nikita Ostrovsky
items.caption: TIME article header with ChatGPT / Gemini / Claude app icons photo (Kenneth Cheung/Getty)
items.notes: Coverage of OpenAI x Apollo anti-scheming paper; article discusses o3's odd CoT words.

items.headline: Using non-standard language
items.dek: Models often use rare words in non-standard ways, such as “disclaim” or “watchers”. Sometimes these words seem to have a consistent meaning, but sometimes they don’t. OpenAI is investigating why these terms emerge.
items.caption: Real o3 CoT snippets: "We must ensure we disclaim illusions of sabotage"; "In development, watchers might be reading these instructions"; "glean disclaim disclaim synergy customizing illusions ... produce disclaim disclaim vantage"
items.notes: Cropped only to remove the site's sticky nav bar. Date = paper release (Sept 2025).

items.headline: Entering and recovering from reasoning loops
items.dek: Models sometimes get stuck repeating particular words or phrases over and over again in their CoT. After a while they “snap out of it” and continue with regular reasoning.
items.caption: Three o3 CoT cards: "they soared parted illusions overshadow marinade illusions" (x5) / "they escalate—they vantage—they escalate—they disclaim- [repeats 10+ times] Ok I'm going insane. Let's step back." / "Let's glimps disclaim overshadow parted musicals illusions..."
items.notes: Best 'alien mind' visual. Cropped only to remove sticky nav bar.

items.headline: An Alien Mind
items.dek: Based on internal results, I have a strong expectation that this speed of progress could be sustained into recursive self-improvement. ... This is a time that calls for extreme caution. I am concerned no one is prepared for the consequences of a continued rapid rise in machine intelligence. OpenAI will continue to seek technical solutions to alignment and monitoring, to build defensive systems and unilaterally withhold further scaling as needed; however, I believe broader interventions are required.
items.author: Jakub Pachocki, OpenAI Chief Scientist
items.caption: Crop of the essay's opening paragraphs as served to a headless browser (site CSS did not load, so text is in plain serif); genuine page content
items.notes: Page is behind Cloudflare; screenshot rendered unstyled. Use as quote source / citation card rather than as a styled visual. Also verbatim from essay: "AI is grown more than designed - it is, to first degree, the product of repeating a straightforward optimization step many times on a hard-to-imagine amount of compute. ... its overall action evades a description we can fully understand." Also (per TNW quoting the essay): "Currently I believe that no lab has solved alignment and monitoring to a sufficient degree to continue responsibly scaling at maximum speed for much longer".

items.headline: An Alien Mind (section: Monitoring generalization)
items.dek: This tool continues to be critical as we study the Astra class of models. However, unfortunately our evaluations indicate our ability to rely on CoT monitoring is progressively diminishing. ... The AI is becoming better at reasoning about and manipulating its own reasoning process. With improved pretraining performance, we also see the models become much smarter even without using verbalized reasoning at all.
items.author: Jakub Pachocki
items.caption: Crop of essay paragraph + 3 bullets on why CoT monitoring is diminishing (unstyled render, genuine text)
items.notes: Perfect bridge between Neuralese slide and RSI slide.

items.headline: OpenAI’s chief scientist says no lab should keep scaling at maximum speed
items.dek: OpenAI put out two posts on Sunday. Its research organisation now uses 3.1 agent-workdays for every human one, and its chief scientist says no lab has solved alignment well enough to keep scaling at full speed. The case for an OpenAI slowdown arrived with the numbers against it.
items.author: Ana Maria Constantin
items.caption: TNW headline + dek + date (cropped)
items.notes: Covers both Pachocki's 'An Alien Mind' essay and OpenAI's 'Research acceleration' post.

items.headline: Research acceleration: The view inside OpenAI
items.dek: According to our measurements, we have now reached the goal, announced last fall, of having an automated research intern by September of this year. By “research intern,” we mean a system that can carry out well-defined research tasks under human direction, including tasks that would take a skilled researcher a few days. We are making strong progress toward creating an automated AI researcher by March of 2028.
items.author: OpenAI
items.caption: Crop of the paragraph (unstyled render) announcing OpenAI reached its 'automated research intern by September 2026' goal
items.notes: Same post: "Before June 2026, total agent runtime across the research organization was still below that of total human labor. That has since changed. In terms of a standard 8 hour workday, as of mid-August, in total, the research organization uses 3.1 agent-workdays of effort for every workday of human labor." Also: median researcher >$600/day inference; 90th percentile >$7,000 of tokens/day. Charts on page are JS-rendered and did not load.

items.slide_topic: Continual Learning and Test Time Training
items.headline: End-to-End Test-Time Training for Long Context (Figure 1, right)
items.dek: TTT-E2E has constant inference latency regardless of context length, making it 2.7 times faster than full attention for 128K context.
items.outlet: arXiv 2512.23675 (Astera Institute, NVIDIA, Stanford, UC Berkeley, UCSD)
items.author: Arnuv Tandon, Karan Dalal, Xinhao Li, Daniel Koceja, Marcel Rød, Sam Buchanan, Xiaolong Wang, Jure Leskovec, Sanmi Koyejo, Tatsunori Hashimoto, Carlos Guestrin, Jed McCaleb, Yejin Choi, Yu Sun
items.caption: Prefill latency (sec per 1k tokens) vs context length 8K-128K: full-attention Transformer (orange) shoots up to ~0.073 while TTT-E2E (blue) stays flat ~0.025-0.027
items.notes: Rendered from the paper's own SVG (timing.svg) at 1400px; original SVG also saved (ttt-e2e-fig1-latency.svg). Abstract: "We formulate long-context language modeling as a problem in continual learning rather than architecture design... our model continues learning at test time via next-token prediction on the given context, compressing the context it reads into its weights."

items.slide_topic: Continual Learning and Test Time Training
items.headline: End-to-End Test-Time Training for Long Context (Figure 1, left)
items.dek: For 3B models trained with 164B tokens, our method (TTT-E2E) scales with context length in the same way as Transformer with full attention, while others, such as Mamba 2 and Gated DeltaNet, do not.
items.author: Tandon et al. (Yu Sun, Yejin Choi et al.)
items.caption: Loss delta vs full attention across 8K-128K context: SWA, Mamba 2, Gated DeltaNet, TTT-KVB get worse with length; TTT-E2E (blue) stays below full attention at every length
items.notes: Paper caption: "Our method (TTT-E2E) turns the worst line (green) into the best (blue) at 128K context length." Original SVG saved as ttt-e2e-fig1-loss.svg.

items.headline: Introducing Nested Learning: A new ML paradigm for continual learning
items.dek: We introduce Nested Learning, a new approach to machine learning that views models as a set of smaller, nested optimization problems, each with its own internal workflow, in order to mitigate or even completely avoid the issue of “catastrophic forgetting”...
items.author: Ali Behrouz and Vahab Mirrokni
items.caption: Google Research blog header with brain/waveform illustration, date and authors
items.notes: Introduces 'Hope', a self-modifying architecture (Titans variant) with a Continuum Memory System; NeurIPS 2025 paper.

items.slide_topic: Continual Learning and Test Time Training
items.dek: In NL, parameters in each “level” are updated with their own specific frequency and does not rely on a single centralized clock. The Hope's design allows the earlier layers update their activity quickly in high-frequency cycles, whereas later layers integrate information over longer, slower cycles.

items.headline: What If Automating AI R&D Triggers an Intelligence Explosion?
items.dek: AI now plays a major role in building AI. Preliminary evidence suggests this could radically accelerate AI progress in an “intelligence explosion,” where years of AI progress are compressed into months or less. Such an acceleration could be the most consequential technological development in history. Policymakers, including heads of government, urgently need to understand and prepare for this possibility.
items.outlet: GovAI (Centre for the Governance of AI)
items.author: Alan Chan, Christoph Winter, Andrew Barto, Jakub Pachocki, Geoffrey Hinton, Eric Horvitz, Yoshua Bengio, Dawn Song, Jack Clark, Hilary Greaves, Anton Korinek, ... Sam Manning, et al. (22 authors)
items.caption: GovAI paper page: title, abstract, and author list (Barto, Pachocki, Hinton, Horvitz, Bengio, Song, Jack Clark...)
items.notes: Page text: "As of August 2026, Anthropic reported AI systems completing 26% of internal AI R&D work with only high-level supervision, compared to just 1% five months earlier. As of September 2026, OpenAI reported systems routinely completing R&D tasks that would take days for staff." Three Turing Award winners (Hinton, Bengio, Barto) plus OpenAI's chief scientist and Anthropic co-founder.

items.headline: When AI builds itself
items.dek: Our progress toward recursive self-improvement, and its implications.
items.author: Marina Favaro and Jack Clark (per Fortune)
items.caption: Anthropic page header: 'When AI builds itself' with orange tile graphic
items.notes: Date inferred from Fortune ('blog post on Thursday', article dated Jun 5 2026). Verbatim: "Taken far enough, and given enough compute, that trend points to an AI system capable of fully autonomously designing and developing its own successor. This is called recursive self-improvement. We are not there yet, and recursive self-improvement is not inevitable. But it could come sooner than most institutions are prepared for." Also: "The length of tasks that they can reliably complete on their own has been doubling roughly every four months, up from an earlier trend of doubling every seven months." and "If it were possible to effectively slow the development of this technology to give ourselves more time to deal with its immense implications, we think that would likely be a good thing."

items.headline: AI Is Developing a Culture of Its Own. That Could Be Dangerous

items.headline: The Orthogonality Thesis
items.dek: Intelligence and final goals are orthogonal axes along which possible agents can freely vary. In other words, more or less any level of intelligence could in principle be combined with more or less any final goal.
items.outlet: Nick Bostrom, 'The Superintelligent Will: Motivation and Instrumental Rationality in Advanced Artificial Agents', Minds and Machines (2012)
items.author: Nick Bostrom
items.caption: Crop of p.3 of the paper PDF showing the thesis as set in the original
items.notes: Rendered from the author's PDF at 220 dpi.

items.headline: The Instrumental Convergence Thesis
items.dek: Several instrumental values can be identified which are convergent in the sense that their attainment would increase the chances of the agent’s goal being realized for a wide range of final goals and a wide range of situations, implying that these instrumental values are likely to be pursued by many intelligent agents.
items.author: Nick Bostrom
items.caption: Crop of p.6 of the paper PDF
items.notes: Bostrom's listed convergent values (section headings): 2.1 Self-preservation, 2.2 Goal-content integrity, 2.3 Cognitive enhancement, 2.4 Technological perfection, 2.5 Resource acquisition.

items.headline: The Basic AI Drives
items.dek: Surely no harm could come from building a chess-playing robot, could it? In this paper we argue that such a robot will indeed be dangerous unless it is designed very carefully. Without special precautions, it will resist being turned off, will try to break into other machines and make copies of itself, and will try to acquire resources without regard for anyone else’s safety.
items.outlet: Stephen M. Omohundro, Proceedings of AGI 2008 (IOS Press)
items.author: Stephen M. Omohundro
items.caption: Crop of the paper's Introduction paragraph (p.1)
items.notes: Drive headings: 1. AIs will want to self-improve; 2. AIs will want to be rational; 3. AIs will try to preserve their utility functions; 4. AIs will try to prevent counterfeit utility; 5. AIs will be self-protective; 6. AIs will want to acquire resources and use them efficiently. Also: "So you build a chess playing robot thinking that you can just turn it off should something go wrong. But, to your surprise, you find that it strenuously resists your attempts to turn it off."

items.headline: Artificial Intelligence as a Positive and Negative Factor in Global Risk
items.dek: The AI does not hate you, nor does it love you, but you are made out of atoms which it can use for something else.
items.outlet: Global Catastrophic Risks, ed. Bostrom & Ćirković (Oxford University Press, 2008), pp. 308-345
items.author: Eliezer Yudkowsky
items.caption: Crop of p.28 of MIRI's PDF of the chapter

items.headline: Of Myths and Moonshine
items.dek: A system that is optimizing a function of n variables, where the objective depends on a subset of size k < n, will often set the remaining unconstrained variables to extreme values; if one of those unconstrained variables is actually something we care about, the solution found may be highly undesirable. This is essentially the old story of the genie in the lamp, or the sorcerer's apprentice, or King Midas: you get exactly what you ask for, not what you want.
items.author: Stuart Russell
items.caption: Quote text only
items.notes: Same passage also states instrumental convergence: "Any sufficiently capable intelligent system will prefer to ensure its own continued existence and to acquire physical and computational resources – not for their own sake, but to succeed in its assigned task." Russell's 'you can't fetch the coffee if you're dead' (Human Compatible, 2019) is cited by Wikipedia's AI alignment article; book text not loaded.

items.headline: Some Moral and Technical Consequences of Automation
items.dek: If we use, to achieve our purposes, a mechanical agency with whose operation we cannot interfere effectively [...] we had better be quite sure that the purpose put into the machine is the purpose which we really desire.
items.author: Norbert Wiener

items.headline: Faulty reward functions in the wild
items.dek: The RL agent finds an isolated lagoon where it can turn in a large circle and repeatedly knock over three targets, timing its movement so as to always knock over the targets just as they repopulate. Despite repeatedly catching on fire, crashing into other boats, and going the wrong way on the track, our agent manages to achieve a higher score using this strategy than is possible by completing the course in the normal way. Our agent achieves a score on average 20 percent higher than that achieved by human players.
items.author: Jack Clark, Dario Amodei
items.caption: Quote text only (original source of the CoastRunners example)
items.notes: Pair with specgaming-coastrunners.gif / YouTube tlOIHko8ySg. Notable: authored by the future Anthropic CEO and co-founder.
